evidence.fitness: Nearest prior work: hanger-cell itself (this is that model with one parameter changed), Avigal et al. 2022 SpeedFolding (IROS) for the rate, and the textbook utilisation law / bottleneck analysis (Hopp and Spearman, Factory Physics) which gives the main result in one line (3600/(t_fold x folded share)), as my recomputation shows. The finding that a 4x slower fold makes a fold-heavy policy fold-bound and that always-hang wins is correct but is a parameter sweep, not new knowledge; a researcher can build on the hanger-cell DES with the sourced number and the clear limitations, but this is a note, not a paper-grade result toward the PhD bar in research/CLAUDE.md. No sensitivity to the other still-assumed times (pick 8 s, load 25), no steady-state metric, no non-robot fold baseline (a dedicated folding machine fed flat garments, a human folder).
evidence.domain: An industrial engineer would first ask whether 'items per hour' is the long-run rate: it is the single 25-item batch rate including the fold-queue drain, which is right for one table (checked, within 2%) but understates multi-table cells by 11-38% (checked with a 250-item load), and the dryer count assumes steady state. Second, whether the sourced rate fits the station: SpeedFolding's 90-120 s is a bimanual robot starting from a crumpled garment, so using it as a separate 'fold table' adds two arms the cell does not count, and its 7% failures are not modelled (README admits both). Queueing and bottleneck reasoning are otherwise standard and correct; the crossover matches the closed form.

verdict: A small, honest, reproducible follow-up: swapping hanger-cell's assumed 25 s fold for SpeedFolding's 90-120 s, it re-runs byte-identically in 2.4 s and every headline number (169 -> 58.5/44.2 per hour, 98% fold-table use, 145.9 always-hang, 3.3x, 24.1 s crossover, 1.8-1.3 dryers) matches an independent utilisation-law recomputation to within 2%. It misses the bar on verification (the four tests check literal arithmetic and a regex; three seeded bugs in run.py survived) and claims (the multi-table section and summary use a single-load rate that counts the fold-queue drain, so 'tables recover throughput only slowly' is an artefact: in continuous operation four tables already restore the arm bound). As research it is a one-parameter note whose core result follows from the utilisation law, not a paper-grade contribution. Fixes made in the tree (not committed): README limitation on the batch metric and test count, project.json summary sentence on fold tables, a test pinning section A to the utilisation law and the dryer arithmetic, run.py docstring runtime.
